title: Two Polygons, One Circle
statement: A regular $12$-gon and a regular pentagon are inscribed in the same circle and share a vertex $A$. Let $S$ be the set of all vertices of these two polygons. A convex polygon is called admissible if all of its vertices lie in $S$, $A$ is one of its vertices, and the following holds for each of its vertices $P$: going clockwise around the circle from $P$, the next vertex of the convex polygon is either the first vertex of the $12$-gon strictly after $P$ or the first vertex of the pentagon strictly after $P$. How many admissible polygons have every interior angle at least $120^\circ$?
hints: Measure each point of $S$ by its clockwise arc from $A$, so the points are the multiples of $30^\circ$ and $72^\circ$ up to $360^\circ$. An admissible polygon is then a route from $0$ to $360$. Write down the arc lengths it can use, and look at the two arcs meeting at each vertex.

By the inscribed angle theorem, a vertex between arcs $a$ and $b$ has interior angle $\frac{360^\circ-a-b}{2}$, so the condition is $a+b\le 120^\circ$ for each pair of adjacent arcs, including the pair at $A$. The only violations occur when a $72^\circ$ arc leaves a pentagon vertex and the arc entering that vertex is too long.

The adjacent arcs that sum to more than $120^\circ$ are $72^\circ$ arcs leaving a pentagon vertex after these entering arcs: $72$ at $72$; $72$ or $54$ at $144$; $72$ or $66$ at $216$; $72$ at $288$; $72$ or $60$ at $A$. Use recursion: go through the points in order, and at each pentagon vertex count separately the routes that may and may not leave by a $72^\circ$ arc. Handle the two possible first arcs separately, because the first arc interacts with the last arc at $A$.
solution: Label each point of $S$ by its clockwise arc from $A$. The labels are the multiples of $30$ and of $72$ up to $360$, and $360$ is $A$ again. Admissible polygons correspond to routes $0\to360$ in which each step goes to the next multiple of $30$ or the next multiple of $72$. Every step is at most $72$, so every route has at least $5$ arcs and gives a genuine polygon. If the arcs on either side of a vertex are $a$ and $b$, the angle there is $\frac{360-a-b}{2}$. It is at least $120^\circ$ exactly when $a+b\le120$. The possible arcs are $6,12,18,24,30,36,42,48,54,60,66,72$. Here $54$ occurs only as $90\to144$, $60$ only as $300\to360$, and $66$ only as $150\to216$. A pair fails only if the sum exceeds $120$. A $72$ arc starts at a pentagon vertex, so a non-$72$ arc after it is at most $30$. The $66$ arc is followed by $24$ or $72$. Hence the forbidden adjacent pairs are exactly these: $72$ then $72$; $54$ then $72$ (at $144$); $66$ then $72$ (at $216$); and the closing pair at $A$ of last arc $60$ with first arc $72$. Call a route free at a pentagon vertex if it may leave by a $72$ arc, and blocked otherwise. Write $(\text{free},\text{blocked})$. A $72$ arc makes the route blocked at the next pentagon vertex. First arc $30$. The closing pair is never a problem. The counts are $f(30)=f(60)=1$ and $72:(2,0)$. Then $f(90)=f(120)=3$, and $144:(3,5)$. Then $f(150)=f(180)=f(210)=11$, and $216:(22,14)$. Then $f(240)=f(270)=47$, and $288:(94,22)$. Then $f(300)=f(330)=163$. Routes reach $360$ from $288$ only if free ($94$), from $300$ ($163$) and from $330$ ($163$). This gives $420$ routes. First arc $72$. The route must end $330\to360$, since $60$ is forbidden before it and a $72$ arc is forbidden before it, while $48$ and $18$ do not occur before $A$ in a way that avoids passing $330$ or $300$. The point $72$ is blocked, so $f(90)=f(120)=1$ and $144:(1,1)$. Then $f(150)=f(180)=f(210)=3$, and $216:(6,4)$. Then $f(240)=f(270)=13$, and $288:(26,6)$. Then $f(300)=f(330)=45$, giving $45$ routes. The total is $420+45=465$.

solution_figures.alt: Circle with a regular 12-gon and a regular pentagon inscribed, sharing the vertex A at the top. Each of the 16 points of S is labelled with its clockwise arc in degrees from A: multiples of 30 and of 72. The pentagon is dashed. One admissible polygon is drawn in bold, visiting 0, 30, 72, 90, 144, 150, 216, 240, 288, 300 and back to A.
